abstract: |
 The length- and age-structure of commercial landings is a crucial input to fish stock assessment. In the Northeast United States, NOAA Fisheries deploys samplers to fish dealers to measure the length of commercially landed fish.  When there are few or no samples of a market category of fish, the informational content of fish prices can be used to make an inference about the size of an unsampled market category. We use the Black Sea Bass fishery in the Northeast United States to illustrate our approach to using economic data to inform stock assessments.  There are 5 common market categories: Jumbo, Large, Medium, Small, and Unclassified.  From 2020 to 2023, 5 to 10% of commercial landings were in the “Unclassified” market category but no fish in this category were measured. A preliminary hedonic model confirms that prices vary by market category: “Unclassified” Black Sea Bass are priced between “Large” and “Medium” fish. We fit a categorical Random Forest to predict the probability that a transaction belongs to a particular market category using prices and other variables.  We use the results to predict the probability of the “Unclassified” belonging to any of the other market categories, allowing us to construct a price-informed length structure of commercial landings.

# Introduction


<!--- Include the next 2 child documents.   --->
```{r, child=here("writing", c("summary.Rmd")),  eval=FALSE}
```

From 2014-2024, no fish in the "Unclassified" market category of Black Sea Bass (*Centropristis striata*) landed from the south subunit were  measured by portside biosamplers in the Northeast United States.  From 2020-2024, no Unclassified fish in the north region were measured either.  This left a gap in the data necessary to  to construct the age-structure of commercial landings, itself a crucial input to the quantitative 
stock assessments in the Northeast United States. The stock assessment enterprise in the Northeast U.S. has a series of business  rules for handling gaps that arise when certain market categories are not sampled or under-sampled. In this article, we describe an approach that harnesses the information contained in the price of fish to fill this data gap.  The intuition is straightforward.  Because the the demand for  fish depends on individual body size, the equilibrium market price provides a signal about individual fish size.  

In the Northeast US, commercial fishing vessels catch fish and sell their landed fish to dealers. The catch is sorted
into market categories. The NOAA Fisheries deploys biological samplers to measure the length of commercially landed fish. 
Otoliths are collected and aged from a subset of measured fish. For black sea bass and many other stocks, these data are used
to convert the landed weight of all market categories into numbers-at-age of commercial landings. 

As part of our exploratory data analysis, we estimate a hedonic model to confirm that prices vary by market category. We tune, train, and validate a random forest model that classifies sales transactions into one of the four primary market categories. Our ultimate goal is to improve the stock assessment enterprise by including more information about the true size of un-measured "Unclassified" fish. This requires  predictions of the Unclassified fish to be aggregated to the year-stock unit level and the accuracy of an individual prediction is of no interest.  We use the model to predict out-of-sample on Unclassified fish and compare the resulting price-informed age structure to the baseline age-structure constructed using methods idential to the most recent stock assessment.

## Catching, Classifying, and Selling  Fish

Black sea bass are commercially caught by fishing firms that typically use bottom trawl and
pot/trap gear; gillnets and hook-and-line are less commonly used. Firms can target both
sizes of fish and their catch of other species, but cannot perfectly control 
what they catch and land.  The ability to target, and therefore the size composition of landings, is impacted by fishing regulations, which vary by state, and environmental conditions. For example, the seasonal inshore movement during 
the spring and offshore movement  during the fall [@Moser2009] can affect the composition of landings.  When fish are offshore, they are
less available to smaller vessels and those that are registered in states that 
manage with stringent possession limits.  Strong year classes can make a size 
class temporarily more available during certain years.


The fishery is jointly managed by the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission (ASMFC) and the Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council (MAFMC). Regulations are enacted by NOAA Fisheres. From 1996 through 2003, the fishery was managed primarily by quarterly catch limits for the entire fishery. There were early closures in 1999 (Quarters 2,3,4), 2000 (2,3,4), and 2001 (all). Quota was allocated to each state starting in 2003 (Amendment 13) and is monitored based on the state in which catch is landed. States are required to enact commercial regulations that will result in state level landings that are less than or equal to it's quota allocation. In 2021, the formula that allocates commercial quotas to the states was revised; 75% of the quota is allocated according to historical  fishing and 25% is allocated in proportion to where the biomass is located.

Firms operating in federal waters must hold a federal permit; fishing vessel operators are required to report information about fishing trips, including gear used, fishing location, landing locations, and estimates of the weight catch of each species. They are also required to sell their catch to federally permitted dealers, who report information that be used to link to the vessel reports along with value (nominal dollars) and landed weights (to the nearest pound)^[This has implications for units in subsequent analysis]. These purchase reports are disaggregated by market category.  There is some catch that occurs within state waters by fishing vessels that do not have federal permits. 

Although all states have enacted some form of Limited Access, there is substantial variability in management across the states. Three states (Maryland, Delaware, and Virgina) currently manage the fishery with an Individual Fishing Quota (IFQ) program, while the other states manage with varying combinations of minimum size limits, possession limits, and season closures.  Possession limits vary widely by state; the IFQ states do not have  possession limits while Massachusetts and Rhode Island use seasonally varying limits that have been as restrictive as 50 lbs/day or as liberal as 1,500 lbs per week.


```{r length-histograms,echo=FALSE,out.width="48%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center',fig.cap="Length and Real (2023Q1 USD) Price Frequencies by market categories, 2013-2024."}
knitr::include_graphics(c(here("images","background","LenFq.Mktcomb.pdf"),here("images","exploratory","wprice_histograms_vertical_NR.pdf")))
```

Fishing vessels catch fish and deliver the catch to buyers (fish dealers).  Dealers report purchase quantities and value by market category to NOAA Fisheries.  This market structure, in which the quantity and quality supplied is determined before prices adjust to equalize quantity supplied and quantity demanded, is common in fish markets [@Barten1989; @Kristofersson2007;@Gobillon2017].  There are four prevalent market categories (Jumbo, Large, Medium, and Small), plus an "Unclassified" category^[Following the stock assessment, "Mixed or Unsized" is aggregated with "Unclassified";  "Extra Small" and "PeeWee" are aggregated with Small category; "Extra Large" is aggregated with "Jumbo"].  Figure \@ref(fig:length-histograms) illustrates that fish in the "Unclassified" category are precisely that, an unobserved combination of the other market categories. No standardized definition of the market categories exists and the definitions themselves may vary over time (year-to-year, month-to-month) and geography (state-to-state or stock area to stock area).  Many fish dealers act as wholesalers, selling whole fish to processors, restaurants, or final consumers. Other fish dealers are vertically integrated with some downstream entities, processing and selling filleted fish to downstream customers. Vertical integration, in which a firm has control of the harvest and dealer activities also occurs, for these observations, it is unclear that prices reported are truly equilibrium prices. 

The market categories exist because downstream buyers care about the sizes of fish; prices of most types of fish depend on the size of fish. Prices are also influenced by other attributes, including freshness, fat content, water content, buyer- and seller- effects, and the quantity supplied to the market^[@McConnell2000, @Carroll2001, @Kristofersson2004, @Kristofersson2007,  @Lee2014, @Hammarlund2015,  @Gobillon2017, and @Ardini2018 are just a few examples.]. 

Prices can be used to predict market category only if prices actually vary by market category. Figure  \@ref(fig:length-histograms) suggests that is the case and a simple hedonic model verifies that prices do indeed vary by market category (Table \ref{HedonicMarketCats}).  The hedonic model is fit by ordinary least squares. In addition to the presented coefficients, the model contains controls for gear, landed state, year, month, daily landings, and daily landings$^2$.  All but the final two terms are factor variables that are "one-hot" encoded. 
 The price of Jumbo black sea bass is approximately \$13.08 per kg, while the price of small black sea bass is approximately to \$7.46 per kg.  The Unclassified market category has an average price of \$7.46 per kg, in between that of Large and Medium fish, suggesting that unclassified fish may be a mix of these other two categories^[A hedonic price model is not the main focus of this research, nevertheless, we report more details about the simple model in the Appendix.].

## Black Sea Bass and the Stock Assessment Enterprise 

### Stock assessment 


Black sea bass are protogynous hermaphrodites, reach maturity around 2-3 years old, live approximately 8-12 years, and change sex from female to male in older, larger ages.
They exhibit seasonal movement patterns, overwintering offshore in the fall and winter in deeper waters but returning to inshore waters in early spring to spawn. They prefer to
aggregate in structured habitats and are caught near reefs and wrecks. Though black sea bass north of Cape Hatteras are managed as a single stock, a distinction is drawn around Hudson Canyon that subdivides this stock into a northern and southern subunit with assumed, though minimal, movement between these groups which has been confirmed through tagging studies [@Moser2008].

 Since 2023, the black sea bass stock assessment model has used an age-based Woods Hole Assessment Model (WHAM) with northern and southern subregion [@Miller2025].^[Before 2023, reference points used by the MAFMC and ASFMC were derived from two Age Structured Assessment Program (ASAP) models, one for the subunit north of Hudson Canyon and one for the subunit south of it.]  Movement between the northern and southern subregions is estimated, with a strong prior derived from a priori tagging data [@Miller2025]. Each subunit has distinct assumed life history input like weight at age, length-weight relationships, and maturity at age. The assessment model also estimates distinct parameters for each subunit including abundance, recruitment, fishing mortality, and selectivity. Because the recruitment is distinct, the subunits can have noticeably different size compositions, and the northern subunit had large age classes in 2012 and 2018. 

The assessment model is fit to catch data from the commercial and recreational fishery, and two sources of fisheries-independent indices: model-based indices from a VAST model [@Thorson2019; @Hansell2026] and recreational catch-per-angler indices. The conversion from raw catch data to catch-at-age necessitates using portside and observer sampling data of lengths and ages (via otoliths). Because such data can be highly spatiotemporally variable, these data are aggregated to the year, semester (Jan-Jun or Jul-Aug), and region (north or south).

### Port Sampling for Ages and Lengths 

A port sampling program has existed in the northeast United States for more than three decades,
collecting vital biological data like lengths, weights, ages, and stomach samples that directly support
the fisheries stock assessment process. Sampling is done by professionally trained samplers using electronic measuring boards, scales, and otolith extraction to measure and store the information, often bringing samples back to central locations for further analysis like aging.

Throughout its history, the program has been staffed by federal port agents or contracted companies, and funded by the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS).
Because staffing and financial resources are limited, sampling priorities been rigidly set through a two-stage  prioritization system.  In the first stage, stocks 
with analytical assessments, high average recent landings, and high profiles are allocated more samples.  In the second stage, the stock assessment lead uses their knowledge of the fishery and assessment to request samples from particular regions, times of year, and market categories.  These decisions heavily influenced by availability of historical data, timing and location of
commercial landings, spatio-temporal abundance of the stock, and stock assessment model.

From 2015-2019, the portside biosampling program employed 7 full-time port samplers and collected over 200,000 samples annually. Due to budget reductions and staff attrition, by 2024 fewer than 50,000 lengths were collected by 3 full-time and 3 part-time samplers.
The biosampling efforts have been supplemented by partners and stakeholders, like MAFMC and the state of Massachusetts.  A recent merger of the portside sampling program with the NEFSC observer program is anticipated to increase efficiency and sampling, lowering the travel, training, and sampling costs. This merger is also expected to increase the efficiency and better logistics coordination, to reduce the number of trips samplers need to take from their homes to ports, though this process is still laborous and costly.

Biosamplers try to meet the sample requests by traveling to ports at times where a variety of species and sized fish are likely to be landed. They may also travel to a specific port to fulfill the scientific requests for a particular species, stock, or market category. When these requests are unfulfilled, the resultant data gaps necessiatate changes in the stock assessment. Modelers will relax the specificity of the information, i.e., borrow across regions or semesters, and in extreme cases may take length and age distribution data from fisheries-independent sources rather than from the catch subsamples. However, it is preferable to have unbiased and precise
sample information to convert the total landings in pounds to landings-at-age, which are necessary for age-based stock assessments like WHAM.


```{r LenHist2,echo=FALSE,out.width="32%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center',fig.cap="Length Frequencies by market categories, 2009-2024."}
knitr::include_graphics(here("images","background",c("LenFq.Mktcomb.Region.Color.2009-2013.png","LenFq.Mktcomb.Region.Color.2014-2018.png", "LenFq.Mktcomb.Region.Color.2019-2024.png") ))
```

Figure \@ref(fig:LenHist2) illustrates these data gaps and their attendant problems; there are no biosamples for Unclassified fish in the South region after 2013 and very few in the north, particularly after 2018^[All measured Unclassified fish in the 2019-2024 time period came from a 2 week time period in a single port in 2020.  There are also relatively few samples of Jumbo in the South from 2014-2018 and Small in the North from 2019-2024.].  In all three time periods, landed fish tend to be slightly smaller in the South region relative to the North region, reflecting differing regional tendencies for grading.  Filling data gaps in the South with data from the North is therefore likely to produce catch-at-length estimates that are too large. Within a region, borrowing data from an adjacent market category is also likely to produce poor estimates of catch-at-length.  For the Unclassified category, it is not clear which market category is adjacent.  Borrowing data from adjacent time periods also may be problematic from both theoretical and empirical perspectives. Unclassified black sea bass must be allocated to an age category in order to conduct an age-structured stock assessment, but without any additional information Figure \@ref(fig:LenHist2) leaves the stock assessment scientists in an uncomfortable place. 



# Methods and Data


## A Stylized Theoretical Model Guides Our Modeling Approach 

The goal of this research is to use the information contained in transaction level prices to infer something about the size of the Unclassified fish.  Three fundamental facts guide the modeling approach. First, a perfectly competitive market for fish implies the Law of One Price: homogenous goods will have identical market equilibrium prices.  Second, that heterogeneous composite goods can be unbundled into their constituent attributes using a hedonic model and when competitive markets for attributes exists, these attributes will have identical market prices. Third, that all models, including those of markets are only approximations to reality.


### The Competitive Market Equilibrium and the Law of One Price

The existence of a competitive market for black sea bass is critical to our ability to use prices to infer market category.  It ensures that the prices capture all relevant quality information and that there is a single price^[All identical goods will sell at the same price; therefore observations of identical goods with different prices *suggest* that some conditions of a competitive market are absent [@Lamont2003].  Variations of the law of one price that account for heterogenous goods, informational assymmetries [@Salop1982], and different data availability have been proposed and tested statistically [@Asche1999; @Nielsen2009; @Pettersen2018].].  The intuition behind the law of one price is straightforward.  A dealer that offers less than the market equilibrium price, will purchase no fish; fishing firms would sell to another dealer.  A dealer that offer more than the market equilbrium price will purchase all the fish and this new "too high" price becomes the new equilibrium price.

Many conditions are required for a perfectly competitive market to produce a single price. It requires many "small" buyers and sellers, no vertical integration, no transactions costs, and complete information.  Markets with many buyers and sellers ensures that no individual can singularly influence the equilibrium price.  No vertical integration ensures that all trades are true arms-length transactions.  A lack of transactions costs means that completing a sale and looking for a counterparty is costless, this enables firms to search for the best price.  Complete information assures that all buyers and sellers know the quality attributes of every lot of fish and the preferences of all the other agents.  Under these conditions, the market prices encapsulate all relevant information.  <!--- We also assume there is no vertical integration between dealers and vessels: a dealer and a fishing vessel is not owned by the same firm and there is no "forward" contracting in which buyers and sellers agree in advance on a price. 
A simple theoretical model sketch can provide guidance about explanatory factors that belong in the model. --->

To build intuition, we temporarily make three further assumptions. First, with the exception of market category, we assume that all fish are identical.  Second, dealers face a downstream customer with a perfectly elastic demand for each market category. Together, this implies constant prices  for each market category, regardless of the quantity landed and delivered to the market. Third, we assume there are two  categories of fish: Jumbo and Large. The downstream consumers strictly prefer Jumbo to Large, so the market equilibrium price of Jumbo is strictly greater than the equilibrium price of Large: $p^J > p^L$.  Finally, the Unclassified category is a composite of the two and $\alpha_i$ is the proportion of transaction $i$ composed of Jumbo. 

Buyers and sellers have full information and can observe the proportions of Jumbo and Large in any Unclassified transaction. Therefore, we can perfectly deduce the underlying composition of the Unclassified transaction, because the equilibrium price of Unclassified transaction $i$ is:

\begin{equation}
\label{unknown1}
p_i^U= \alpha_i p^J+ (1-\alpha_i) p^L \hspace{2mm} 
\end{equation}.


<!---We assume that dealers have a perfectly elastic demand curve for the two categories of fish, Jumbo and Large, and that they prefer Jumbo relative to large.  A perfectly elastic demand curve means that dealers will buy all Jumbo landings as long as the price of Jumbo is less than or equal to $p_J$. The same holds true for the Large market category. --->

The assumptions of a perfectly elastic demand curve for each market category and that transactions are identical are unrealistic for many reasons. In this application, sales transactions are of similar, but not identical goods.  The goods vary along many dimensions, including size, method of production, and time and location of landing. Meat quality can vary within a season, resulting in different prices within a year.  Regional differences in transportation costs, processing costs,  or final consumer preferences and incomes can produce in regional variation in prices [@samuelson1954transfer; @Krugman1991a].  The demand curve for nearly all fish is downward sloping: increases in quantity supplied will reduce prices [@Kristofersson2004; @Kristofersson2007; @Lee2014; @Ardini2018].
<!---
The hedonic model (Table \ref{HedonicTableA}) suggests these attributes impact prices.  Because many attributes impact prices, transactions of different size classes may have similar prices.  This suggests that attributes that are important in determining the price of fish should enter as factors in the classification model. Intuition for this can be seen in the following example based on the Table \ref{HedonicTableA}. Most fish are delivered "Round," dead with the gut in.  Some fish are delivered live, these receive a premium of approximately \$0.16 per kg. The mean price of a Small Live black sea bass is \$8.07 (=\$7.46 +\$0.61), which is very close to the mean price of Medium Round \$8.14.  Without including an indicator for Live, a machine learning model would be likely to classify "Small Live" black sea bass as "Medium."

A perfectly competitive market is convenient myth of economics and we should not expect the law of one price to hold perfectly and unconditionally.  That is, all black sea bass does not trade at the same price; however, black sea bass with similar attributes will trade at similar prices.  Therefore the classification model should include factors that explain variation in prices.  These include attributes like gear used, whether the fish is sold live, state of landing, daily quantity landed, and time period of landing. -We should expect the prices of similar goods to be more similar than prices of different goods, although a working definition of similar can be tricky.  In particular, instead of adding prices to the random forest model directly, we use prices to construct a distance metric between the transaction and "typical" price of each market category. ## Modeling Probability of Class Membership with a Random Forest

The black sea bass stock assessment requires and estimate of landings aggregated at the year-, semester-, and region; therefore, our goal is to generate accurate prediction of the true market category of the Unclassified fish at that aggregation.  Neither the accuracy of an individual prediction nor the causal mechanisms by which one factor affects market category is of interest.  Machine learning approaches, which focus on accurate prediction of an outcome variable instead of the causal relationship between predictors and outcome, are attractive methods [@Varian2014; @Mullainathan2017; @Athey2019].  These approaches have proliferated in fisheries, ecology, and economics [@Rubbens2023; @Kuhn2024; @Akselrud2024]. Applications include from classifying fishing activity with Vessel Monitoring Systems or Autotmatic Identification Systems [@Russo2011], building predictive models of fishing vessel trip costs [@Chan2021] and prices [@francca2024price], and image processing [@Alvarez-Ellacuria2020].

In this application, we use a multinomial random forest model [@Breiman2001; @Malley2012] to model the probability that a transaction is in one of the four principle market categories^[Random forest pplications of these models in fisheries include classification of acoustic data [@Fallon2016, @Proud2020], fishery metiers [@Oostdijk2024], and habitat [@Liu2025].].  Random Forests can be viewed as ensembles of Classification and Regression Trees [CART, @Breiman1984].  A classification tree repeatedly partitions observations into two groups based on a single explanatory variable.  The optimal factor to use and partitioning value is selected by minimizing a measure of variation among member of the partition; we use gini impurity.  The CART algorithm grows tress by continuing to split until all branches are homogenous or an early stopping criteria is met. 

Single classification trees are prone to poor out of sample performance; a tree grown to pure nodes is perfectly fit to the training dataset.  Random forests improve out of sample prediction by bootstrapping and restricting each bootstrap replication to a small number of randomly selected predictors [@Breiman2001; @Strobl2009; @Hastie2023 ].  Both modifications induce variation in the individual classification trees.  Motivated by Equation \ref{unknown1}, we treat the random forest as a probability machine by averaging over the final notes of tress to assign probability of class membership [@Malley2012; @Kruppa2014].

Like many machine learning models, random forests have hyperparameters which must be exogenously supplied. Results can be sensitive to these choices; models are typically tuned by searching for an optimal set of parameters using a subset of data and the selected parameters are validate model on a holdout sample.  Averaging methods, including Random forest models, are also known to be underconfident; high probabilities are understimated and low probabilities are overestimated.  This occurs because the model averaging process in which individual trees are aggregated into random forests averages away extreme values.  Calibration through an auxiliary model, is often necessary after fitting a random forest [@Niculescu-Mizil2005; @Kull2017; @Ojeda2023; @Barreada2024; @Ferrer2025].

Our model training procedure attempts to account for these idiosyncracies of Random Forest models. We split our dataset three ways; we use 70% of our dataset to tune the model hyperparameters, 15% to calibrate probabilities, and 15% to validate the model. We grow 500 trees when tuning the model and when training the final model.  The number of randomly selected predictors (*mtry*) is tuned over in nearly all Random Forest applications. Simulation studies by @Barreada2024 suggest tuning over the minimum node size (*min.n*) when using random forests in probability models. We tune over these two hyperparameters by performing a 10-fold cross validation study. We grid search over the reasonable starting values of the two parameters.^[The initial grid search used a space filling grid and searched 24 points on $mtry \in (5,35)$ and $min_n \in (5,100)$.  Preliminary analysis showed that the optimal $mtry$ was well above 5 and that a local optimal might be at 100, therefore we adjusted the ranges to (10,35) and (10,300) respectively, and changed the grid size to evaluate 120 points.]  We supplemented the initial grid search by performing the bayesian tuning described by @Shahriari2016.  Our cross-validation was stratified by market category to ensure that the proportion of each class in the folds approximately matched the initial compositions. We selected the optimal pair of hyperparameters that had the smallest log loss criterion function averaged over the ten folds. For each fold, log loss is computed as: 

\begin{equation}
\label{logloss1}
LogLoss = - \sum_{i=i}^N Y_{ik} ln(Pr_{ik})
\end{equation}
where $i$ indexes observations, $k$ indexes classes, $Y_{ik}=1$ if observation $i$ is a member of class $k$, and $Pr_{ik}$ is the predicted probability that observation $i$ is a member of class $k$.

After selecting the best hyperparamters, we refit the model on the entire 70% tuning dataset.  We use the fitted model to predict class membership for the 15% calibration sample. We visually assess whether the model is well-calibrated using commonly used calibration plots [@Ojeda2023; @Barreada2024]. We also use the Relative Calibration loss methods described in [@Ferrer2025] to assess whether calibration is necessary (it is) and to select among isotonic, beta, and multinomial calibration methods.

We apply the the trained model and the probability calibration routine to the final 15% of our data as a final validation, and all model fit results are based on the calibrated probabilities. The random forest model is fit in R using the ``ranger`` package; we use  ``tidymodels`` packages to facilitate tuning, training, and out-of-sample predicting.  

After training the model and calibrating probabilities, we predict out of sample on the Unclassified Landings.  We 
use the trained model to predict the probability of class memembership^[The alternative is to assign class membership to the highest predicted class] and aggregate the corresponding live weight to the year-, market category-, and subregion level.  We then convert these adjusted landings to an age structure and compare it with the traditional age structure. 



## Data, Pre-Processing, and Feature Engineering

We use Catch Accounting and Monitoring System (CAMS)^[Documentation at https://apps-garfo.fisheries.noaa.gov/cams/index.html] data from 2013 to 2024 to train our model. The CAMS data compiled by GARFO consists of dealer transactions matched to vessel trip reports. Dealer data are transaction-level reports of fish purchases by federally permitted fish dealers from each vessel.  They are disaggregated to the trip and market category level and include landed weight (pounds) and value (nominal US Dollars).  Prices are converted to Real 2023Q1 values using the CPI for all urban consumers (CPIAUCSL). Vessel trip report data are reports of fishing activity by federally permitted vessels that are disaggregated to the statistical area-gear-trip level and include information about area fished, gear used, trip length, and estimates of quantity kept (hail weights) and discarded at the species level.   Matching is performed based on the Vessel trip report serial number. When this match fails, matching is done based on the vessel permit number, dealer identifier, and date which are contained in both the vessel reports and the dealer reports.  When vessels fish in multiple statistical areas or using multiple gears, they file more than one report per trip.  One of the functions of the CAMS data system is to allocate trip-level dealer records to the appropriate statistical area.  CAMS allocates in proportion to the hail weights on those trip reports, splitting a single trip record into multiple observations.

Black Sea Bass may be caught by firms without a federal fishing permit and sold to dealers without a federal dealer permit.  In some states, firms without a federal permit can fish for black sea bass in state waters (within 3 miles of land) and sell it to fish dealers who do not have a federal permit.  These sales are also in our data and the CAMS system imputes both statistical area (area adjacent to landing port) and gear used when missing. 

Our observational units are these allocated sales transactions; the dependent variable is the market category and explanatory variables include transformations of price and other variables that impact prices.  In the exploratory analysis (the hedonic model presented in Table \ref{HedonicTableA}) and the Random Forest, we frequency weight the observations by the landed weight in pounds^[We use pounds, instead of kilograms, because the data are reported in integer pounds, and frequency weighting requires integers.].  This treats our observations as if they were repeated observations of the sale of a pound of fish.  We do this for a few reasons.  First, they are exactly that.  Second, we are not interested in predictions of aggregate transactions; our goal is to obtain a prediction of aggregate weight prediction of the true but  unobserved market category of Unclassified fish.   Frequency weighting affects our methods in a few ways. We use log-loss as the criterion function for tuning and calibration; the log-loss function is modified to weight each observation by pounds. During the fitting of the individual trees, observations are drawn with replacement in proportion to their frequency weight. This results in bootstrap samples which more closely resemble the frequency weighted data instead of the raw, unweighted data.

Economic theory described in the theoretical model and on-the-ground subject-matter expertise (the black sea bass stock assessment and commercial fishery) guide explanatory factors, factor engineering, selection of data, and validation procedures [@Mullainathan2017]. 

Machine learning algorithms can often benefit from preprocessing data and factor engineering. Missing values for predictors are handled by splitting the data as if they didn't exist, assigning the observations with missing values to each nodes, and selecting the node that has the greatest decrease in impurity.  We treat factors variables as "unordered" and follow the implementation method described in @Hastie2009.  Unlike many other machine learning models, Random Forest models are scale invariant; explanatory factors do not need to be centered at zero or scaled to have similar variances. Except for prices, all explanatory factors enter the model in raw form. 

We operationalize the Law of One Price by constructing a "prevailing price" for each market category and state as the weighted moving average over the previous 14 days. There are some periods where not sales are observed for a particular market category and day. When this occurs, we impute a price based on a regional price and a state's average premium or discout to that regional price.  We enter the difference between a transaction's price and the prevailing price for Jumbo, Large, and Medium market classes, we do not include a price difference relative to Small. During the exploratory analysis phase we also experimented with including untransformed prices.  

The buyers (dealers) are the entities that report the market category of fish and are likely to have an unobserved propensity to grade fish into particular classes.  This unobserved heterogeneity guides two modeling decisions. Traditional estimators often use a set of one-hot  indicator variables to account for individual-specific effects; doing so in Random Forests can lead to both overfitting [@Breiman2001; @Hastie2023] and bias [@Strobl2007; @Strobl2009]. Target-encoding collapses these indicators to one per class and minimizes this problem; in this application we would modify the typical target-encoding procedure by constructing annual, dealer-specific weighted class probabilities
and enter these, lagged one year, as predictors instead. 

@Roberts2017 note that standard cross-validation techniques are overly optimistic when observations are dependent, as they would be with this type of unobserved heterogeneity.  This occurs because the hold out data used for cross-validation is not actually independent. @Roberts2017 suggest that the practical implications of this depend on the purposes of the model; if prediction on "similar" data is the goal, then a standard cross-validation may be appropriate.  We believe this is the case: we observe records of sales from vessels to dealers, train our model on a subset (the Classified transactions) of those data, and predict out of sample on the remaining Unclassified transactions. At every point in the process, we are able to observe the dealer and it's propensity to grade or purchase particular market categories^[If, however, our objective was to predict class membership for new dealers, the standard cross validation could lead to overly optimistic training results and poor out of sample prediction].

The theoretical model sketch also guides inclusion and exclusion of data used to train the Random Forest. Observations for which prices are formed in a manner inconsistent with our theoretical model are removed  from the training dataset. We exclude observations where pricing information in our data may be form in a way that is not consistent with the theoretical model.  We can think of three scenarios where this is likely to occur.  

First, there is less quality assurance and quality control for the species value field which we use to construct prices. While there are checks to ensure that the values are within a reasonable range, firms that do not report accurately may not be required to improve their reporting accuracy. We handle this by excluding transactions with prices that are too high (over \$15 per pound) or too low (under \$0.15 per pound).  Second, buyers and sellers may be owned by the same entity, and the reported *ex-vessel* prices are likely to be insensitive to market forces.  Fully disentangling ownership is difficult, but inspection of the data suggested that some dealers-vessel pairs were exclusively trading with each other, suggesting some vertical integration.  Third, firms may also participate in forward contracting in which the price of fish is determined well in advance of landing.  To account  for the final two, we excluded transactions from dealer-year-market category combinations where the standard deviation of prices was less than 0.10.  Table Summary statistics describes characteristics of the full dataset and the cleaned dataset.


```{r BSB_data, eval=T, echo=F}
#stack together the data_split, tagging by partition
estimation_dataset <- bind_rows(
  training(data_split)   %>% mutate(partition = "train"),

)

my_selection<-c("priceR_CPI","lndlb")



count_obs<-  estimation_dataset %>%
      group_by(market_desc) %>%
      summarise(n = n(), total_mt = sum(lndlb/lbs_per_mt, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
      pivot_longer(
        cols = c(n, total_mt),
        names_to = "variable",
        values_to = "value"
      ) %>%
      pivot_wider(
        names_from  = market_desc,
        values_from = value
      ) %>%
      mutate(
        variable = if_else(variable == "n", "N", variable),
        stat = "",
        across(-c(variable, stat), ~as.character(round(.x, 1)))
      ) %>%
  relocate(variable, stat, Jumbo, Large, Medium, Small)


summary_numerics<-estimation_dataset %>%
  group_by(market_desc) %>%
  summarise(across(
    all_of(my_selection),
    list(
      mean = ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
      se   = ~sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(.x)))
    )
  )) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -market_desc,
    names_to = c("variable", "stat"),
    names_sep = "_(?=[^_]+$)"
  )%>%
  mutate(value = if_else(stat == "se", paste0("(", round(value, 3), ")"), as.character(round(value, 3)))) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = market_desc,
    values_from = value
  ) %>%
  arrange(variable, stat) %>%
  mutate(variable = if_else(stat == "se", "", variable))%>%
    relocate(variable, stat, Jumbo, Large, Medium, Small)

summary_numerics<-summary_numerics %>%
  bind_rows(count_obs) %>%
  select(-stat)

) %>%

# Results

Our procedure is to tune two hyperaparameters using 75\% of our dataset, calibrate on 15\%, and validate on the final 15\% holdout sample. We present results of the initial tuning, calibration, and validation.  To summarize, the initial tuning found optimal hyperparameter values of $mtry=25$ and $min_n=161$ respectively.  The calibration steps find moderate gain from isotonic calibration, and the validation shows the model fits well. The tuning and validation model fit statistics are similar, suggesting the model is not overfit.  Although the model is not a causal one, the importance of explanatory factors in the Variable Importance Plots make intuitive sense.

## Tuning and Calibration results


```{r rocTune,echo=FALSE,fig.show='hold', fig.align='center',fig.cap="ROC curves from tuning"}
knitr::include_graphics(here("results","ranger","tune", glue("roc_tune_nocluster{pred_vintage}.pdf")))
```

In-sample ROC curves from tuning are quite similar across folds
and the initial steepness indicates the tuned random forest fits well (Figure  \@ref(fig:rocTune)).  The random forest model performs exceedingly well for the small market category, despite the small market category being relatively rare in the data. The model performs worst at classifying the Large market category; referring back to  (Figure \@ref(fig:length-histograms)) illustrates the relatively high degree of overlap between the prices of Large with its neighboring Medium and Jumbo market categories.  

```{r vip,echo=FALSE,fig.show='hold', fig.align='center',fig.cap="Variable importance measured as mean decrease in accuracy from permutation of each predictor. Top 20 of predictors shown"}
knitr::include_graphics(here("results","ranger","final", glue("vipnocluster{pred_vintage}.pdf")))
```

The VIP confirms that the three price variables are the most important in predicting market category (Figure \@ref(fig:vip)) and the four measures designed to capture the Dealer propensities to purchase particular categories are the next most important factors.

The calibration step (Figure \@ref(fig:calibrationplots)) illustrates an issue that commonly affects predictions of Random Forest models. A well calibrated model will be close to the 45 degree line.  For three of the four classes, the aggregation of individual trees leads to underconfidence; observations with high predicted probabilities have even higher true probabilities. The exception is the Small market category; this may be indicative of class imbalance in the dataset.  The isotonic regression used to calibrate predictions corrects much, but not all, of the model underconfidence and improves the log loss (Equation \ref{logloss1}) by approximately 5\% (from 0.526 to 0.497).^[We experimented beta and multinomial logistic calibration, but isotonic regression performed the best]

```{r calibrationplots,echo=FALSE,fig.show='hold',out.width="48%", fig.align='center',fig.cap="Plots of true event rates versus predicted event rates for raw predictions (left panel) and predictions calibrated with an isotonic regression (right panel)."}
knitr::include_graphics(here("results","ranger","final", c(glue("cal_windowed_nocluster{pred_vintage}.pdf"),glue("cal_isovalidate_windownocluster{pred_vintage}.pdf") ) ) )
```


## Testing Results

After tuning the hyperparameters, training a final model, and estimating an auxiliary calibration model, we predict class membership for the holdout sample.  These figures illustate out-of-sample model performance. The ROC curve in Figure  \@ref(fig:roc-Valid) is similar to the those produced by tuning model, suggesting we are not overfitting the model. 

```{r roc-Valid,echo=FALSE,fig.show='hold', fig.align='center',fig.cap="Calibrated ROC curves for the Testing Sample.  The trained model is used to predict probabilty of class membership and those probabilities are calibrated before construcing the ROC curve."}
knitr::include_graphics(here("results","ranger","final", glue("testing_calibrated_roc_curvenocluster{pred_vintage}.pdf")))
```


We also construct a weighted confusion matrix based on for the calibrated model predictions (Figure \@ref(fig:SoftWeightedPredictionHeatmap)).   For each observation in the testing dataset, we multiply landed weight by the each of the class membership probabilities and then aggregate.  This is slightly different than the standard method in which observations are assigned to the class with the highest probability.

# Discussion

No manuscripts would be complete without a discussion of caveats. Here they are.

## General approach

In equation \@ref(unknown1), we develop the intuition behind the model using two market categories and note that we can deduce the composition of the unclassfied transaction based on the price.  However, we have more than two market categories, so the theoretical model is fundamentally underindentfied without additional assumtions.  That is, with four distinct, constant prices ($p_S \leq p_M \leq p_L \leq p_J$), an arbitrary price between $p_S$ and $p_J$ could be constructed with many weighted combinations of prices.  This is slightly troubling in theory, but because there is substantial overlap in sizes even for disparate size categories, it may have minor consequences for aggregate accuracy.  That is, consider a transaction of Unclassifieds that trades at $p_L$, is assigned 100% probability of being Large, but is actually a mix of Medium and Jumbo.  Figure \@ref(fig:length-histograms) suggests the practical implications of this error may be minimal.

<!---
### More that two market categories

When there are more than two market categories (say, Medium), equation \ref{unknown1} becomes:

\begin{align}
p&= \beta_1 p^J+ \beta_2 p^L + (1-\beta_1-\beta_2) \\\label{unknown2}
\sum_{i=1}^3 \beta_i&=1\\
\geq 0 & \beta_i \geq 1 \hspace{2mm} \forall i=1,2
\end{align}
Intuitively, observing a transaction price that falls between two market categories does not imply that a transaction is a linear combination of the two adjacent categories. This suggests that including other proxies for beyond just prices and factors that affect prices is necessary.
--->



## Method critiques 

Predicting out of sample is always difficult. We train the model on Classified observations and then predict out of sample on Unclassified.  This is reasonable if, as we assume, Unclassifieds are a mix of different classes and an efficient market for fish exists. In particular, it assumes that the Unclassifieds can, and are, costlessly classified by the dealer and sold downstream.  This may not be true; it costs time to sort fish, although the marginal cost of sorting borne by the dealer may be minimal.  More troublingly, the Unclassifieds may be systematically different from the Classified fish. We attempt to control for those possible differences by including explanatory factors that may be correlated with quality, and therefore prices, in the model.



Our Random Forest model does very well at predicting observations and comparatively worse at weights (Table \@ref(tab:transaction-predictions and \@ref(tab:weighted-predictions)).  This is a bit surprising; by frequency weighting the bootstrap samples in the Random Forest we expected the opposite to occur.

We use a Random Forest model as a probability machine.  This is a well-known and easy to implement approach. However, the Random Forest does not account for the ordinal relationship between the size classes. Although there is overlap in the length distributions (a particular Jumbo fish might be smaller than a Large), the size categories themselves are ordered, and "Learning to Rank" models may fit better. Alternatively, an alternative loss function used during tuning and traing that penalizes near misses (A Jumbo classified as a Large) less severely than bad ones (A Jumbo classified as a Small) may also improve our aggregate predictions without switching to a different model.

## Extensions

We view this as a reasonable method for generally filling in gaps in historical data.  In addition to the above caveats, one other is warranted. Black Sea Bass prices are approximately monotone in size; larger fish have higher prices.  Using prices as an additional source of information would be difficult if there were a non-monotone relationship between size and prices.

Investigate how to combine existing biosampling data with these pricing information (complement instead of substitute).


In the United States, socioeconomic information has been used in fish stock assessments in limited ways. @chan2022 highlights three entry points for  socioeconomic information in the stock assessment process: data collection, data processing, and parameterizing stock assessment models, stock projections, and understanding effects of policies.  This effort illustrates a novel method of using socioeconomic information in the data processing step.  It also suggests a method for optimizing the collection of portside sampling data. Collecting these data are costly and price information could be a substitute that allows this effort to be reallocated to other stocks and species. Candiates include difficult-to-sample categories when there is size overlap with neighboring categories, prices that depend approximately monotonically on size, and competitive markets for fish.  We specifically caution against forgoing age-sampling to  "end" market categories (Jumbo and Small in the case of Black Sea Bass).

Principal-Agent problem in collecting samples. Contracting firm is paid by sample, firms try to maximize profits and individuals try to maximize utility. Collecting samples from "easy" locations is, by definition, easier and more profitable than meeting difficult requests.

A common entry point is the standardization of Catch-per-Unit Effort metrics to account for changes due to technology [@walters1996, @maunder2004].  These are particularly important for fisheries which do not have fishery independent data collections.  Recently, @vanpoorten2016 illustrate how entry and exit can shape selectivity and @kleiven2022 illustrate how accounting for changing technology impacted abundance estimates for European lobster.

Social science information can be another source of information about catch. Semi-structured interviews with fishing industry participants found that true catch of redfish (*Sebastes mentella*) was at least twice as high as the officially reported catch, which was used to select from competing stock assessment models [@duplisea2018a,@duplisea2018b]. @Gervasi2025 illustrate how similar methods can be used for Gulf Red Snapper in the Southeast United States.

         `Transaction error (%)` = percent((predicted_transactions-transactions)/transactions, accuracy=0.01) )
  

transactions_nocalibrate_predictions<-nocalibrate_results %>%
  select(market_desc,transactions, predicted_transactions, `Transaction error (%)`)%>%
    mutate(
    predicted_transactions = comma(predicted_transactions, accuracy = 0.1),
    transactions = comma(transactions, accuracy = 1)                        
  )

weights_nocalibrate_predictions<-nocalibrate_results %>%
  select(market_desc,true_mt, predicted_mt, `mt error (%)`)%>%
    mutate(
    true_mt = comma(true_mt, accuracy =0.1),
    predicted_mt = comma(predicted_mt, accuracy = 0.1)                        
  )

```

```{r nocalibrate_table, echo=FALSE}




kable(
  transactions_nocalibrate_predictions,
  format    = "latex",
  booktabs  = TRUE,
  digits    = 0,
  caption  = "Uncalibrated Predictions on the Validation Sample (transactions)",
  col.names = c("Market Category", "Actual Transactions", "Predicted Transactions", "Error Rate"),
  escape    = TRUE,         # allows LaTeX in cell content
  label     = "uncal-trans-predictions"
) %>%
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("hold_position"),
    font_size     = 10
  ) 




```


```{r weighted_no_calibrate_predictions, echo=FALSE}

kable(
  weights_nocalibrate_predictions,
  format    = "latex",
  booktabs  = TRUE,
  digits    = 0,
  caption  = "Uncalibrated Predictions on the Validation Sample (mt)",
  col.names = c("Market Category", "Actual Transactions", "Predicted Transactions", "Error Rate"),
  escape    = TRUE,         # allows LaTeX in cell content
  label     = "uncal-weights-predictions"
) %>%
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("hold_position"),
    font_size     = 10
  ) 

```
